messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: default syntax for markdown?
parts:
Hi all,

I feel <!--begin.rcode and end.rcode--> are too long to type, and I
hope the syntax for markdown can be simpler. I'm thinking of this:

#rb label, opt=value
code
#re

rb means "r begin", and re is "r end". Or

#{% label, opt=value
code
#%}

or

#{{ label, opt=value
code
#}}

If you like these ideas or have better proposals, I can change the
default syntax in knitr; otherwise I will keep them for my own use.
Thanks!

Regards,
Yihui
--

parts:
Yi,

I agree that a shorter syntax would be better. I think #rb / #re is
the best of these, . Another idea would be to borrow the syntax from
github/pandoc markdown (http://johnmacfarlane.net/pandoc/
README.html#delimited-code-blocks):

```knitr
code
```
This would allow various markdown parsers to recognize the code as
knitr down the road.

Noam

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: default syntax for markdown?
parts:
The major challenge is the ending pattern of the R chunk, because we
need to be able to decide which blocks are R code, and which are not.
Three backticks ``` can terminate any code blocks, so I think four
backticks may be a reasonable for R code blocks, e.g

``` {r label, opts}
1+1
rnorm(10)
````

```c
/* this is not R code*/
void main()
```

This is valid syntax in both pandoc and GitHub. Does this sound good
to you guys? (chunk.begin='^``` \\{r (.*)\\}$' and chunk.end='^````$')

Regards,
Yihui
--

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: default syntax for markdown?
parts:
I'm not sure that I'm understanding the problem. Beginning line
matches with the next ending line in markdown as long as the number of
backticks match. You cannot chain beginning code chunks like you can
in Sweave.

Could it be possible to have a pattern to detect entire code chunks at
once? such as chunk="^(```+)knitr\\s*([^\\n]*)(.*)^\\1" some care
would need to be taken to ensure that '^' matches beginning of the
line and not just the beginning of the string, which I think is an
option of PCRE. This regex could match and extract the beginning
line, the options and the code, in one go. Slightly different
structure that the beginning line end of line, but it has it's
advantages.

-Andrew

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: default syntax for markdown?
parts:
This is the problem: pandoc and knitr parse the code blocks differently --

- pandoc looks forward and tries to find the ending pattern that
matches with the beginning
- knitr/Sweave does not require the two patterns to be matched, so
they are searched independently, e.g. this is valid in knitr by not in
pandoc:

``` {r}
1+1
``` {r}
rnorm(10)
````

messages.author: 8c8f0ca54c4a2459
messages.subject: Re: default syntax for markdown?
parts:
Experimenting on github wiki, it does not seem that four ticks is
recognized as the end of a code chunk.

Also, if we want to keep both the source and the output as functional
documents, there's a need to reconcile pandoc and knitr's code block/
chunk option syntax. Yihui's proposal won't render correctly in
pandoc with the label and options. Pandoc's code block syntax is:

```{.r .numberlines #label option="x" option2="y"}

From a little trial and error I found that
- option values must be in quotes
- only language names and pandoc options start with a period
- . ".numberlines" can go anywhere,
- r (or .otherlanguage) must go first
- The label requires a # sign
- There are no commas between options.
- Github deals with this syntax just fine

Ideally knitr could use the chunk options for it's own options and
pass unused options to the output hook, as well. However, if this is
too complicated, Yihui's original proposal might make more sense for
now:

```{.r .numberlines}
#rb label, opt=value
Some code
#re
```
This would have the advantage of working across different flavors of
markdown, but the knitr labels would still be part of the source
document. knitr would have to detect if there were code block before
and after the chunk and, if there are, not insert the four spaces at
the beginning of each line.

messages.author: 881c51ed14655bd5
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: default syntax for markdown?
parts:
So I think I worked out a great proof of concept for everything in a
single regular expression. I made a gist at
https://gist.github.com/5a4448e6f4edd925bbc0 where you can see it but
I will repeat it here. The idea uses perl regular expressions with
named chunks. All the patterns combined into one regex so that
matches can be reused. The look ahead operator defines and end chunk
with out capturing the end chunk. If the end chunk is ``` then is
match and consumes it. The named pattern allows for the things to be
extracted by name. I show how to extract the options and body of each
chunk with the chunks chained together.

Chaining the patterns together into a single regex is powerful because
you can match the same number ticks at the end as at the beginning.
It also has the advantage of being much more explicit of an ending.
This way chained chunks can be either allowed or disallowed as a
pattern. There was a trick that I had to do to simulate the multiline
option, since I saw no way to turn that on.

``````r
# Test String
s <- "
# header
```knitr chunk
1+1
```knitr cache=T
2+2
```
more documentation
and some more
"

# Define patterns with named chunks for extraction
head <- "(^|(?<=\\n))(?P<ticks>```+)knitr(?P<options>[^\\n]*)"
body <- "(?P<body>.*?)"
end <- "((?=(?P=ticks)knitr)|(?P=ticks))"

# Combine patterns with newlines between
(pattern <- paste(head, body, end, sep="\\n"))

# extract all matchs
(m <- gregexpr(pattern, s, perl=T))

# Check matches
regmatches(s, m, invert=F)

# extract match start and end points
start <- attr(m[[1]], "capture.start")
length <- attr(m[[1]], "capture.length")

# Extract options Strings
os <- start[, 'options']
oe <- os + length[, 'options']-1
options <- substring(s, os, oe)

# Extract body strings
bs <- start[, 'body']
be <- os + length[, 'body']-1
body <- substring(s, bs, be)
```````

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: default syntax for markdown?
parts:
You are right that four ticks won't work with GitHub wiki, but they
can be rendered correctly in GitHub repositories, e.g.

https://github.com/yihui/knitr-book/blob/master/source/01-introduction.md

I do not know why the wiki system uses another set of syntax.

We do not need to worry too much about the source documents, because
it is the output documents that we really read, and they will be
correctly formatted. The difference between '``` {r label}' and '
#rb label' is that the former will hide chunk options in the GitHub
rendered results, and the latter can show the reader chunk options in
(comments).

Regards,
Yihui

> too complicated, Yihui's original proposal might make more sense for
> now:
>
> ```{.r .numberlines}
> #rb label, opt=value
> Some code
> #re
> ```
> This would have the advantage of working across different flavors of
> markdown, but the knitr labels would still be part of the source
> document.  knitr would have to detect if there were code block before
> and after the chunk and, if there are, not insert the four spaces at
> the beginning of each line.
>

On Sun, Mar 18, 2012 at 9:10 PM, Andrew Redd <amr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> So I think I worked out a great proof of concept for everything in a
> single regular expression.  I made a gist at
> https://gist.github.com/5a4448e6f4edd925bbc0 where you can see it but
> I will repeat it here.  The idea uses perl regular expressions with
> named chunks.  All the patterns combined into one regex so that
> matches can be reused.  The look ahead operator defines and end chunk
> with out capturing the end chunk.  If the end chunk is ``` then is
> match and consumes it.  The named pattern allows for the things to be
> extracted by name.  I show how to extract the options and body of each
> chunk with the chunks chained together.
>
> Chaining the patterns together into a single regex is powerful because
> you can match the same number ticks at the end as at the beginning.
> It also has the advantage of being much more explicit of an ending.
> This way chained chunks can be either allowed or disallowed as a
> pattern.  There was a trick that I had to do to simulate the multiline
> option, since I saw no way to turn that on.
>
> ``````r
> # Test String
> s <- "
> # header
> ```knitr chunk
> 1+1
> ```knitr cache=T
> 2+2
> ```
> more documentation
> and some more
> "
>
> # Define patterns with named chunks for extraction
> head <- "(^|(?<=\\n))(?P<ticks>```+)knitr(?P<options>[^\\n]*)"
> body <- "(?P<body>.*?)"
> end  <- "((?=(?P=ticks)knitr)|(?P=ticks))"
>
> # Combine patterns with newlines between
> (pattern <- paste(head, body, end, sep="\\n"))
>
> # extract all matchs
> (m <- gregexpr(pattern, s, perl=T))
>
> # Check matches
> regmatches(s, m, invert=F)
>
> # extract match start and end points
> start  <- attr(m[[1]], "capture.start")
> length <- attr(m[[1]], "capture.length")
>
> # Extract options Strings
> os <- start[, 'options']
> oe <- os + length[, 'options']-1
> options <- substring(s, os, oe)
>
> # Extract body strings
> bs <- start[, 'body']
> be <- os + length[, 'body']-1
> body <- substring(s, bs, be)
> ```````
>

parts: >>pandoc allows either backtick ` or tilde ~ do both of these have problems?

On a German keyboard, tilde should work; it requires AltGr, but we are used to this because @ also needs it. ^, ´ ` are .... keys (forgot the correct name, I thought it was "dead"). 

However, I was wrong when I said we needed 8 ticks. ```` needs only 4, giving nothing after the first tick, then two ticks after the second.

Sorry for the confusion, we try to avoid these keys if possible, because the behaviour is so strange.
